chunks: "Brushes wear because they're a sliding contact doing several jobs at once, and each job removes a little material. The first cause is mechanical.
The brush is pressed against a moving commutator, so friction slowly abrades it away.
The wear is roughly proportional to the contact force times the distance slid, which is the Archard idea, so higher spring force, higher speed and a rougher commutator all wear it faster.
The second is electrical. Every time the brush bridges segments, the coil is inductive and there's a small spark. That arcing erodes material and roughens the surface.
More current, higher speed and bad commutation make it worse. Even without sparks, current heats the contact spots and weakens the film. The third is chemical and environmental.
Graphite brushes depend on a thin film of copper oxide and adsorbed water to lubricate. In very dry air or at altitude the film breaks down and wear skyrockets.
Oil, silicone and dirt also damage it, and humidity or temperature that's too high or low changes it.
And it's coupled: a worn or out-of-round commutator, or high mica between the segments, makes the brush bounce, which causes arcs, which worsen the surface.
That feedback is how a slowly wearing motor suddenly fails.
Fixes are the right grade, correct spring force, a clean round commutator, suppression, and keeping within the speed and current ratings."
